opus-5.5.text:
I think there were a few moments that really shifted how the field felt, at least from where I was sitting.

One of the earliest for me was the move toward end-to-end learning for manipulation, around 2015 and 2016. The idea that you could train a single neural network to map directly from raw pixels to motor torques, rather than hand-engineering a perception pipeline and a separate controller, was a big conceptual shift. The results were fairly narrow at the time, a robot screwing a cap onto a bottle or putting a block in a shape sorter, but it showed that the deep learning playbook that was transforming vision could plausibly apply to physical control too.

The second turning point was a growing recognition that data was the bottleneck, and people starting to take data collection seriously as a first-class research problem. For a long time the field was very algorithm-centric: if we just found the right reinforcement learning method, things would work. But I think many of us came to realize that the large-scale successes in language and vision came from scale and diversity of data, and robotics just didn't have that. Efforts like large multi-robot datasets, pooling data across many labs and embodiments, and also much better teleoperation setups changed what was possible. Low-cost bimanual systems like ALOHA were a big deal there, because suddenly you could collect high-quality demonstrations of really dexterous tasks, like putting a battery in a remote or tying shoelaces, relatively cheaply. Combined with better policy architectures, things like diffusion policies and action chunking, imitation learning started working much better than people expected.

The third was the arrival of strong vision-language models and the realization that you could build on top of them. Robotics doesn't have to learn everything from scratch anymore. If you start from a model that already understands a lot about objects, language, and the visual world from internet data, and then fine-tune it on robot data, you get vision-language-action models that generalize much better to new objects, new instructions, and new scenes. That made the idea of a general-purpose robot foundation model feel concrete rather than aspirational.

And then I'd say the most recent shift has been seeing these models handle longer-horizon, messier real-world tasks, like folding laundry from a crumpled pile, cleaning up a kitchen, or working in homes they've never seen before. Those are tasks that were essentially science fiction a few years ago. They're still far from perfect, and reliability is a huge open problem, but the gap between what works in a demo and what's needed for real deployment feels like something we can actually close now, which is a very different feeling than the field had even five years ago.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think there are a few. If I go back, one of the first ones for me was actually seeing deep learning work in the context of robot perception and control at all. Around 2015, 2016 we were doing end-to-end visuomotor policies, where you take pixels in and output motor torques, and that was a big deal at the time because the conventional wisdom was that you had to hand-engineer a perception pipeline, do state estimation, and then do control on top of that. The fact that a neural network could learn all of that together, even for a single task on a single robot, was a signal that the paradigm could change.

But honestly, for a long time after that, progress felt slow because everything was so narrow. You'd train one robot to do one task in one lab, and it wouldn't generalize to a different object, let alone a different environment. So I think the second big turning point was the shift toward scale and diversity in data. Things like the RT-1 and RT-2 work at Google, and then the Open X-Embodiment effort, where a bunch of labs pooled data across many different robots, showed that if you train on broad, diverse data, you start to get generalization that you simply couldn't get before. RT-2 in particular, where you take a vision-language model that's seen the internet and fine-tune it on robot data, and it suddenly knows things about objects and concepts it never saw in the robot data, that felt like a moment where the internet-scale pretraining story was actually transferring to robotics.

And then the third one, which I think is what's made it feel really fast recently, is the combination of better low-level policy learning with those foundation-model-style backbones. Diffusion policy was a good example of a method that just made imitation learning work much more reliably for dexterous, contact-rich tasks. And then ALOHA and the low-cost hardware push made it possible for a lot more people to collect good teleoperation data. When you put those together, you get things like pi-zero, where a single model can fold laundry, or bus tables, or do fairly long-horizon tasks that would have seemed out of reach two or three years ago.

So I'd say it's less one single breakthrough and more a sequence: first that learning could work at all in the loop, then that data diversity gives you generalization, and then that pretrained models plus the right policy architectures plus more accessible hardware let you compound all of that. The compounding is what makes it feel fast now.

astra-6.text:
I think there are a couple of things. One is the shift from building a separate system for every task to training a single model on data from many different tasks. Once you do that, you can start to get transfer: learning one skill helps the robot learn another. That makes collecting broader datasets much more valuable, and it changes how you approach the problem.

The other is being able to build on models pretrained on images and language. Previously, you might have needed robot experience to learn both what an object is and how to interact with it. Now you can bring in some of that visual and semantic knowledge and use the robot data to learn how to act.

I wouldn’t point to one moment when robotics suddenly started working. It’s more that those pieces are coming together. We have a much clearer path toward systems that can generalize across tasks, even though reliability and handling unfamiliar situations are still really hard.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one big turning point was the shift from building a separate system for every task to asking whether we could train a robot on many tasks and have it generalize to something new. That changes both how you collect data and what you expect the model to learn. Instead of engineering a solution to one particular problem, you’re trying to build a system that can reuse what it’s learned.

And then the progress in language and vision models has been really exciting for robotics. Those models can bring in knowledge that would be very expensive to acquire entirely through a robot’s own experience. But there’s still a gap between recognizing something or describing what should happen and actually controlling a robot to make it happen. To me, the interesting progress is in connecting those capabilities to learning from physical interaction.
